title: Quantized Neural Network Accelerator
notes: Our project studies a proposed accelerator for the matrix calculations inside a small digit-recognition network. We compare 32-bit floating-point values with 8-bit integers. The focus is the relationship between numerical precision, memory traffic, and the processing lanes that perform the calculations. This is a high-level software architecture model. We count its matrix-stage cycles and separately measure prediction accuracy; we did not build or measure a physical chip.
reference: High-level software model · matching workload and resource assumptions

title: What we built and why
notes: The architecture question is whether smaller operands can reduce storage and execution costs while preserving useful predictions. We implemented checked arithmetic, a configurable cycle-stepped matrix engine, and a NumPy neural-network workload, then connected the experiment exports to the graphs. Brevitas informed our quantization choices, including separate scales for weights, activations, and biases. FINN informed our thinking about parallelism and memory organization. Those are design references: we did not install either framework or claim that our simple sequential engine reproduces FINN. Our contribution is the custom implementation and its verification and evaluation.
reference: Design references: Brevitas and FINN · detailed links in the backup slides

title: The workload: handwritten digits
notes: MNIST is a collection of small grayscale pictures of handwritten digits, each supplied with a correct label from zero to nine. Each image has 28 by 28 pixels. We normalize the pixels to the range zero to one and flatten them into 784 inputs. Our network has 64 intermediate values and ten final digit scores. ReLU between the layers replaces negative values with zero. The largest output score selects the digit. The two matrix products require 50,176 and 640 multiply-accumulates, for 50,816 MACs per image. A MAC means multiply two operands and add the product to a running total. This prepared workload lets us connect an actual network to a manageable architecture model.
reference: Source: MNIST test archive · network dimensions and counts from mnist-results.json

title: Configure first. Test separately.
notes: We split the original training archive into 54,000 training images, 5,000 validation images, and 1,000 calibration images. A separate archive contains the 10,000 test images. Training learns the weights and biases; validation monitors learning. After training, calibration chooses the hidden activation scale without using correct-answer labels or updating weights. A scale tells us what each stored integer represents. We observe the largest nonnegative first-layer value on those calibration inputs, divide by 127, and freeze that scale. The input scale comes directly from the known zero-to-one pixel range. The test images then grade the configured model. The correction here was which images choose the scale. Both the earlier and corrected versions kept it fixed while predicting; the earlier version incorrectly used the test set to choose it.
reference: Source: notebook 05 data split and calibration procedure · seed 530

title: Keep the arithmetic in integer units
notes: The network already has learned biases, which are offsets added to each layer's matrix result. We did not invent new biases. We convert them once to INT32 in the same units as the integer products. In this illustrative example, integer 20 with scale 0.01 represents 0.20. A learned bias of 0.04 becomes integer four in those units, so the addition is 20 plus four equals 24. If the next layer uses scale 0.04, that result becomes integer six: both represent 0.24. That is rescaling, rather than a simple cast. Our actual hidden conversion uses integer multiplier 464,594 and a 30-bit shift with ties-to-even rounding. The multiplication uses an INT64 temporary, the hidden values are stored as INT8, and final scores remain INT32. Floating point is still used during training, calibration, and conversion of prepared pixels at the input boundary.
reference: Illustrative values above · actual rescaling uses multiplier 464,594 and shift 30

title: Our proposed matrix accelerator
notes: An accelerator is hardware specialized for a kind of computation. Our proposed machine specializes in matrix multiply-accumulate operations. External memory holds inputs and weights. A local buffer holds one resident matrix stage, and the lanes calculate separate output dot products. The baseline has eight lanes, 256 KiB of local storage, and 32 bytes per cycle for both local operand reads and external transfers. The clock is assumed to be 100 MHz. The buffer fits the largest FP32 stage without tiling, which keeps both precision cases comparable. Each lane can issue one MAC per cycle if data is available. Load, compute, and store phases do not overlap. We reload weights for every layer and image. Dedicated result-write ports and the absence of banking conflicts are simplifying assumptions, and equal lane counts do not imply equal physical area or power.
reference: Assumptions: one MAC/lane/cycle · sequential load/compute/store · no tiling or banking conflicts

title: One answer, six clock cycles
notes: Before using the neural network, we check a calculation we can do by hand: two times four, plus three times five, plus one times six, equals 29. With one INT8 lane, the three input bytes load in one cycle and the three weight bytes load in another. There are three compute cycles because the lane performs one MAC per cycle. The four-byte INT32 result then stores in one cycle. That gives six cycles, or 60 nanoseconds at the assumed 100 MHz clock. The general model rounds the input, weight, and output transfers separately, then adds the scheduler's compute cycles. Larger matrices may stall if the local read budget cannot supply every lane. This example demonstrates that our simulator counts an explicit schedule while performing the arithmetic; it does not just assign a speedup factor to INT8.
reference: Source: notebook 03 known-answer trace · one-lane INT8 example at the assumed 100 MHz

title: Verify computation, then assess accuracy
notes: We checked actual image values and trained weights through both simulated layers on the first 16 test images. The second layer receives the simulated first-layer result after the required bias and activation steps. Integer products match wider independent calculations exactly. FP32 results match with a fixed tolerance because NumPy and our sequential multiply-add model can use different summation orders. The largest final-score difference was about 0.0000038. Every sampled prediction matches its numerical reference. Image eight is especially useful: its known digit is five, but both versions guess six. The simulator is still correct because it reproduces the network's calculation. Classification accuracy is a separate measurement on all 10,000 images. Tuong will now discuss that accuracy and the performance tradeoffs.
reference: Source: mnist-results.json verification rows · FP32 rtol 1e−5 / atol 1e−4

title: Accuracy stayed close in this run
notes: On all 10,000 test images, FP32 correctly classified 9,696 and the calibrated integer version correctly classified 9,698. That is 96.96 percent versus 96.98 percent, a difference of only 0.02 percentage points. There were 15 different predictions between the two versions. The net gain of two correct answers does not mean only two predictions changed, and it does not show that INT8 is inherently more accurate. Quantization changes rounding and can move close scores in either direction. The mixed-precision reference and the integer core selected the same digits on this run, even though their arithmetic representations differ. This is one small network with one fixed training recipe, so the supported conclusion is that this calibrated representation retained similar accuracy for this workload.
reference: Source: mnist-results.json accuracy counts · full 10,000-image test set

title: Smaller operands reduce matrix-stage cost
notes: The baseline matrix stages require 19,204 cycles for FP32 and 8,025 for INT8. The ratio is 2.393. The darker bar segments show computation: 12,736 FP32 cycles versus 6,400 INT8 cycles. The lighter segments show transfers: 6,468 versus 1,625 cycles. Both formats have the same one-MAC-per-lane issue rule. Smaller integer operands reduce transfer cost and allow more MACs through the same local read budget. Resident matrix storage falls from 204,096 to 51,216 bytes, while external traffic per image falls from 206,952 to 51,960 bytes, both reductions of about 75 percent. Outputs remain 32 bits, so these totals do not drop by exactly fourfold. Bias and scale metadata are excluded from the matrix-only counts. These timing estimates also exclude bias, activation, rescaling, and digit selection.
reference: Baseline: 8 lanes / 32 B per cycle buses / 100 MHz · matrix stages only; biases and scales excluded from traffic

title: More lanes eventually wait for data
notes: This experiment changes only lane count while keeping both bandwidths at 32 bytes per cycle. INT8 improves from four to eight to 16 lanes, but 32 lanes give the same cycle count as 16. Each INT8 MAC needs two one-byte operands. A 32-byte local read budget therefore supplies at most 16 MACs per cycle. FP32 needs two four-byte operands, so the same connection supplies at most four MACs per cycle. This explains why the FP32 curve is nearly flat and why the INT8 curve eventually plateaus. Output grouping also matters: the second layer has ten outputs. With eight lanes, it needs a group of eight and then a group of two, with unused lanes in the final group. More arithmetic hardware does not automatically improve execution when data supply or the schedule limits it.
reference: Source: accelerator-results.json lane_sweep · both bandwidths fixed at 32 B/cycle

title: External bandwidth reduces transfer time
notes: Here we fix 32 lanes and vary external bandwidth from eight to 128 bytes per cycle. The local read budget remains 32 bytes per cycle. The INT8 compute portion stays at 3,200 cycles, while transfer time falls from 6,495 to 408 cycles. Total time therefore falls from 9,695 to 3,608 cycles. The highest tested matrix-stage rate is about 27,716 image-equivalents per second at 128 external bytes per cycle. This sweep improves loading and storing; it does not remove the separate 16-MAC-per-cycle local read cap during computation. The two bandwidths affect different phases. This is a modeled rate for the matrix stages, not complete predictions per second, and it does not establish that the highest-bandwidth design is the best physical implementation.
reference: Source: accelerator-results.json external_bandwidth_sweep · 32 lanes / 32 B/cycle local reads

title: The tradeoffs and limits still matter
notes: The similar accuracy does not eliminate tradeoffs. Quantization rounds values, and 34 of the 640,000 test hidden values were clipped. We need calibration, scale metadata, converted biases, rescaling logic, and overflow checks. More lanes can also sit idle behind a bandwidth limit. Our numerical experiment covers one small fully connected MNIST network and one training recipe. The 16-image simulator check demonstrates integration; it is not a second full-test accuracy measurement. Our timing excludes the additional steps needed for a complete prediction. We do not model physical timing closure, area, energy, memory banking, overlap, or persistent weight reuse. The next extension should account for the excluded operations before claiming a whole-inference speedup. Wider workload studies, tiling, unsigned activations, and INT4 would be further work.
reference: Scope: one MNIST MLP / one recipe · no physical area, power, or achieved-clock measurements

title: Balance precision with data supply
notes: The main result is that calibrated INT8 retained similar accuracy while reducing the modeled cost of the network's matrix stages. At the baseline assumptions we observed 96.98 percent accuracy, a 2.393-times matrix-stage speedup, and roughly 75 percent lower matrix storage and external traffic. We implemented the numerical path and scheduling model ourselves, verified real network calculations, and connected exported experiment results to the graphs. The scaling studies show that precision, lane count, local reads, external transfers, and scheduling have to be considered together. Our conclusion is specific to this workload and high-level model. The backup slides contain bandwidth calculations, integer details, execution evidence, and sources for questions.
reference: Baseline estimates: 8 lanes / 32 B/cycle buses / assumed 100 MHz · accuracy covers 10,000 test images

title: Operand supply limits
notes: The MAC supply limit is local bytes per cycle divided by bytes per operand pair. The actual issue rate also cannot exceed the lane count. This does not model SIMD within a dot product. Output-group barriers matter: the ten-output layer takes two 64-step groups at eight INT8 lanes, not the idealized 640/8 = 80 cycles. This is a scheduler assumption; it is not FINN folding behavior. At 16 lanes all ten outputs fit at once. FP32 has a four-MAC/cycle bus cap, so group tails and arbitration produce the reported 192 versus 160 second-layer compute cycles.
reference: A MAC reads two operands · local read budget = 32 bytes/cycle

title: Integer bias and rescaling
notes: Both biases were learned during FP32 training. The first is converted using input scale times first weight scale; the second uses hidden scale times second weight scale. They are stored as INT32, not INT8. A conservative weight-sum bound covers partial sums and bias addition before the NumPy integer products. The scalar simulator checks each MAC as well. Integer rescaling approximates the positive ratio input_scale × weight1_scale / hidden_scale. ReLU removes negative totals, a checked INT64 product holds the multiplication, quotient and remainder implement ties-to-even rounding, and clipping produces the next INT8 hidden array. Output scores all share one positive scale, so argmax can operate directly on INT32 scores.
reference: Source: mnist-results.json quantization metadata · range −127…127 / zero point 0
